unit.title: Managing your portfolio
unit.description: Rebalance, keep an eye on costs, invest little by little, measure properly and write your plan

steps.title: Why it drifts
steps.body:
Your plan is 60 % shares and 40 % bonds. If the stock market rises a lot, in two years you can be at 72/28 without having touched a thing. Your portfolio is now **riskier** than what you chose.

Rebalancing means going back to your target allocation: selling a little of what rose most or adding to what fell behind.

steps.title: Three ways
steps.body:
1. **By calendar:** once a year, for example in January.
2. **By threshold:** when one part drifts more than 5 points.
3. **With contributions:** new money goes to whatever has fallen short. You don't sell, so you don't trigger any tax.

With investment funds you can also rebalance through a **fund transfer** (a Spanish «traspaso»), without paying tax.

steps.title: The psychological effect
steps.body: In 2009 or in March 2020, rebalancing forced you to buy shares exactly when fear was at its peak. It's a rule that makes you buy low and sell high without having to guess anything.
steps.key: Rebalancing means going back to your plan: selling some of what rose most and buying what fell behind.
steps.tip: It's the automatic way to buy cheap when everyone else is selling.

steps.title: The example
steps.body:
You invest **€10,000** for **30 years** and the market returns 7 % a year (an example, not a promise):

• With no costs: **€76,123**
• With 0.2 % (index fund): **€71,968**
• With 1.5 % (typical active fund): **€49,840**

1.5 % a year takes more than €26,000.

steps.title: Compare for yourself
steps.body: Put in €300 a month for 30 years and compare 0.2 % with 1.8 % in costs: with a 7 % market you end up with about €351,900 versus about €259,100.
steps.tip: Fees compound too, but against you.

steps.title: All the costs
steps.body: Ongoing charges or TER (in the KID), commission per trade, spread, custody, currency exchange and taxes. John Bogle, founder of Vanguard, summed it up like this: «In investing, you get what you don't pay for».
steps.key: Every point of annual fees eats up a huge part of the result because of compound interest.
steps.tip: 1.5 % a year sounds like nothing. Over 30 years, it's a third of your money.

u30l3.title: Investing with a little: €50 a month

steps.title: A little, but early
steps.body:
You don't need thousands of euros. With **€50 a month** for 30 years, if the market returned 7 % a year (an example, not a promise), you'd put in €18,000 and end up with about **€61,000**. Over 40 years, about **€131,000**.

Time does most of the work.

steps.title: Investing every month
steps.body: Move the price up and down: with the same amount every month you buy more units when it's cheap and fewer when it's expensive.
steps.tip: Investing every month is like climbing stairs: what matters is not stopping.

steps.title: How to do it cheaply
steps.body: With little money, fixed fees weigh heavily: €2 on a €50 purchase is 4 %. Look for index funds with no purchase fee or free regular investment plans, and automate your contribution for payday.
steps.key: Starting early with a little usually counts for more than starting late with a lot.

steps.title: Simple and annualised
steps.body:
**Simple:** (final value − initial) ÷ initial. €2,000 → €2,600 is +30 %.

**Annualised:** the average pace per year. +50 % over 5 years is **not** 10 % a year: it's 8.4 %, because it compounds. Formula: (1 + total)^(1/years) − 1.

steps.title: Time-weighted or money-weighted
steps.body:
• **Time-weighted:** what the fund did, regardless of when you put money in. Used to compare funds.
• **Money-weighted:** what **you** made, based on how much you had in at each moment.

If you put in a lot just before a fall, the fund can make money while you lose.

steps.title: Annualising is compounding in reverse
steps.body: Put €10,000 in at 8.4 % for 5 years: you get to about €15,000, +50 % in total.
steps.tip: Always compare like with like: % a year with % a year.

steps.title: Measuring honestly
steps.body: Subtract fees and taxes, compare with a benchmark index and remember inflation. An app telling you «+40 % since you started» without saying over how many years tells you almost nothing.
steps.key: To compare, use the annualised return; to know how much you made, use the money-weighted one.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: A short document that says **what you do, why, and what you'll do when the market turns ugly**. Big institutional investors have one (the Investment Policy Statement). You can have your own on a single page too.

steps.title: The template
steps.body:
1. Goals («X € in year Y for Z»).
2. Horizon.
3. Emergency fund.
4. Allocation.
5. Products and maximum cost.
6. Automatic contribution.
7. When I rebalance.
8. What I'll do if the market falls 30 %.
9. What I'll never do.
10. Speculation limit (optional).

steps.title: Review it properly
steps.body: Once a year or if your life changes: job, children, home. **Not** because the market has gone up or down. Point 8 is the most important: you decide today, calmly, what you'll do when you're scared.
steps.key: A plan written in a moment of calm is what saves you in a moment of panic.
steps.tip: Write down today what you'll do on the day everyone is scared.

steps.title: The challenge
steps.body:
You have **€10,000** to invest over 20 years (your emergency fund is already set aside). Build a portfolio that's diversified, cheap and that you can defend through a rough patch.

Use everything from this section: allocation based on horizon, several countries, few products, low costs and a small slice for speculation if you want.

steps.title: How to defend a portfolio
steps.body: With arguments, not predictions: «I own thousands of companies from all over the world, 20 % in bonds for the falls, a 0.2 % cost and a written rule for rebalancing». It's an exercise for learning, not a recommendation.
steps.key: A good portfolio isn't the one that rises most in a year, but the one you can stick with for 20 years.

u30l1-1.prompt: Your plan is 60/40 and after a good run you're at 72/28. Rebalancing means…
options: Selling shares or adding to bonds until you're back at 60/40
Buying more shares, since they're doing well
u30l1-1.explanation: You go back to the level of risk you chose when you were calm.

u30l1-2.prompt: You have €10,000: €6,000 in shares and €4,000 in bonds. Shares rise 40 % and bonds stay the same. What percentage of the portfolio are shares now? (round to one decimal place)

u30l1-3.prompt: Following on from the previous case (€8,400 in shares and €4,000 in bonds), how many euros of shares would you need to sell to get back to 60 %?

u30l1-4.prompt: And if you'd rather not sell: how much new money would you need to put into bonds to get back to 60/40?
u30l1-4.explanation: If €8,400 must be 60 %, the total must be €14,000. Bonds: 14,000 − 8,400 = €5,600. You already have €4,000: you add €1,600.

u30l1-5.prompt: Your portfolio has drifted to 75 % shares and 25 % fixed income. Your plan is 60/40. Allocate how it should end up: between 58 % and 62 % in shares.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u30l1-5.explanation: Going back to 60/40 returns the portfolio to the risk you decided on. Educational example, not a recommendation.

u30l1-6.prompt: Match each way of rebalancing with how it works.
u30l1-6.explanation: All three work; with contributions you avoid selling and paying tax.
right: You correct if one part drifts more than 5 points
You review on a fixed date, for example every January
New money goes to whatever has fallen behind

u30l1-7.prompt: March 2020: the stock market has fallen 30 % and your 60/40 portfolio is at 50/50. Your plan says «I rebalance if I drift more than 5 points». What do you do?
options: Wait and see what the news says
Sell all my shares before they fall further
Follow the plan: move money from bonds to shares until I'm back at 60/40
u30l1-7.explanation: Rebalancing during falls forces you to buy cheap. That's why it's so useful… and so hard without a written plan.
feedback: The news in the middle of a panic won't tell you where the bottom is. Your rule has already decided for you.
The exact opposite of the plan. And in 2020 the market got back to its high within about 5 months.
That's what your rule calls for. It's scary, which is why it pays to have it written down in advance.

u30l1-8.prompt: Rebalancing with new contributions avoids paying tax on selling.
u30l1-8.explanation: If you don't sell, there's no gain to declare.

u30l1-9.prompt: If you decide to correct only when one part drifts more than 5 points, you're rebalancing by ____.
u30l1-9.explanation: You can also do it by calendar, once a year.

u30l1-10.prompt: With investment funds in Spain, how can you rebalance without paying tax?
options: By selling and buying on the same day
u30l1-10.explanation: A transfer between funds isn't taxed until you finally cash out. ETFs don't have this advantage.

u30l2-1.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years with the market at 7 %. With no costs you end up with €76,123, and with 1.5 % a year, €49,840. How much have the fees taken?
u30l2-1.explanation: 76,123 − 49,840 = €26,283: more than a third of the result.

u30l2-2.prompt: Same case, but with 1.8 % in costs (a net return of 5.2 %). How much would you have after 30 years? (round it)

u30l2-3.prompt: Putting in €300 a month for 30 years, how much separates 0.2 % in costs from 1.8 %?
u30l2-3.explanation: About €351,900 versus about €259,100 with the market at 7 %.

u30l2-4.prompt: 1 % a year in fees barely matters over 30 years.
u30l2-4.explanation: Because of compound interest, every annual point takes a huge part of the final result.

u30l2-5.prompt: Which costs should you check before investing? Select all that apply.
options: The commission on buying and selling
The fund's ongoing charges or TER
u30l2-5.explanation: Also the spread, custody fees and taxes.

u30l2-6.prompt: The annual cost of a fund or ETF is called ongoing charges or ____.
u30l2-6.explanation: You'll find it in the key information document (KID).

u30l2-7.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years with the market at 7 %. Put them in order from most to least money at the end.

u30l2-8.prompt: Quick: who said «in investing, you get what you don't pay for»?
u30l2-8.explanation: The founder of Vanguard and of the first index fund for retail investors (1976).

u30l2-9.prompt: Your bank offers you a fund with 1.9 % in charges «with a star manager». The alternative is a global index fund at 0.2 %. What do you think?
options: It doesn't matter, the difference is small
The star manager will make up for the fee
They'd need to beat the index by 1.7 points a year, every year, just to break even
u30l2-9.explanation: A high fee is a guaranteed handicap; beating the index is an uncertain hope.
feedback: Over 30 years, that difference can be a third of your money.
According to SPIVA, over 10 years 97 % of European equity funds lagged their index. The star would have to be exceptional… for decades.
Exactly: it's an incredibly high bar that almost nobody clears consistently.

u30l2-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Compare it with its index: if the index rose 12 %, the fund did worse
Then better a fund that charges 3 %
u30l2-10.explanation: Judge a fund against its index and over many years, not on one good year.
feedback: That's it! What matters is how much it leaves you compared with the cheap alternative, year after year.
Charging more doesn't make it rise more. The only sure thing about a fee is that you pay it.
That 10 % is already net of fees, but without them it would have been 11.5 %. And in a year it doesn't rise, you still pay the 1.5 %.
lines: My fund charges 1.5 %, but it's up 10 % this year 🚀
So the cost doesn't matter, right?

u30l3-1.prompt: €50 a month for 30 years at 7 % a year (an example, not a promise). Roughly how much would you end up with?
u30l3-1.explanation: About €60,999, of which €18,000 is your contributions and the rest, compound interest.

u30l3-2.prompt: In that same case, how much money would you have put in yourself in total?
u30l3-2.explanation: €50 × 12 months × 30 years = €18,000. The other €43,000 is generated by time.

u30l3-3.prompt: If instead of 30 years it's 40 (€50 a month, 7 %), roughly how much would you have?
u30l3-3.explanation: Ten more years add only €6,000 more in contributions, but the result more than doubles.

u30l3-4.prompt: You invest €100 a month and the price goes through 10, 8, 5, 8 and €10. You buy 65 units with €500. What's your average price? (two decimal places)
u30l3-4.explanation: 500 ÷ 65 ≈ €7.69: below €10 even though the price started and finished there.

u30l3-5.prompt: You split your €50 a month. Rules: at least 2 products, none above 85 %, at most 5 % in crypto and 10 % in a single share.
u30l3-5.explanation: The core, diversified and cheap; the speculative part, small. Crypto is very volatile and you can lose everything you put in. An example, not a recommendation.

u30l3-6.prompt: Pablo is 22 and wants to wait until he has €5,000 saved before he starts investing «properly». It'll take him 4 years. What do you tell him?
options: That he can start now with a small automatic contribution
That he should wait: it's not worth it with a small amount
That he should put it all into a crypto to reach €5,000 sooner
u30l3-6.explanation: Starting small builds the habit and makes the most of time, which is what counts most.
feedback: Good: he starts the habit and time works for him from today. He can raise the amount later.
While he waits, the money loses out to inflation and he loses years of compound interest.
That's gambling, not investing: he could lose it all.

u30l3-7.prompt: If every €50 purchase costs you €2 in fees, you lose 4 % straight away.
u30l3-7.explanation: 2 ÷ 50 = 4 %. With little money, look for options with no fixed fee per purchase.

u30l3-8.prompt: Does it help or hinder investing with a small amount?
options: A minimum custody fee of €30 a year
A fixed fee of €10 per purchase
Index funds with no minimum amount
Waiting until you have a lot before starting
u30l3-8.explanation: With little money, fixed costs eat up a large part of each contribution.

u30l3-9.prompt: Quick: with a large lump sum, what came out ahead more often in Vanguard's studies?
u30l3-9.explanation: About two times out of three, because the market rises more often than it falls. With a salary, investing every month is the natural thing to do.

u30l3-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Start with €50 and raise it when you earn more: time does the rest
Take out a loan to invest more
You're right, better to spend it
u30l3-10.explanation: A little, started early, goes a long way. What matters is the habit.
feedback: That's the way! What counts most is starting early and not stopping.
Investing with borrowed money turns a fall into a serious problem.
Spending is fine, but €50 a month over decades can turn into tens of thousands of euros.
lines: I can only save €50 a month 😔
I won't get anywhere with that, will I?

u30l4-1.prompt: You invest €2,000 and today it's worth €2,600. What's your simple return?

u30l4-2.prompt: An investment gains 50 % in total over 5 years. What's its annualised return? (one decimal place)
u30l4-2.explanation: 1.5^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 0.084 → 8.4 % a year. It's not 10 %: the interest compounds.

u30l4-3.prompt: An investment doubles in value (+100 %) over 10 years. Its annualised return is…?
u30l4-3.explanation: 2^(1/10) − 1 ≈ 7.2 %. It fits the rule of 72: 72 ÷ 7.2 = 10 years.

u30l4-4.prompt: The return that measures what the fund did, regardless of when you put money in, is the ____-weighted return.
u30l4-4.explanation: It's the one used to compare funds and managers with each other.

u30l4-5.prompt: Match each measure with its use.
u30l4-5.explanation: Each one answers a different question.
right: How much the value has changed in total

u30l4-6.prompt: Laura puts in €1,000, which rises 20 % (€1,200). Then she adds another €10,000 and the portfolio falls 10 %: she ends up with €10,080. How many euros has she made or lost in total? (use a minus sign if she's lost)
u30l4-6.explanation: She put in €11,000 and has €10,080: −€920. The fund, on the other hand, did 1.2 × 0.9 = +8 %.

u30l4-7.prompt: In Laura's case, the fund made 8 % and she lost money. Both things can be true at the same time.
u30l4-7.explanation: Time-weighted: +8 %. Money-weighted: negative, because she had almost everything in right during the fall.

u30l4-9.prompt: An app boasts that your portfolio is «+40 % since you started». You started 7 years ago. A global index fund has returned 7 % a year over that time. How do you rate it?
options: I annualise it: 1.4^(1/7) − 1 ≈ 4.9 % a year, below the index
Better not to look at the return
u30l4-9.explanation: A total figure without a timeframe says nothing. Annualise it and compare with a benchmark index.
feedback: Without the timeframe you can't tell: over 7 years, 40 % is less than 5 % a year.
Exactly. Only by annualising can you compare, and here the comparison doesn't come out well.
Measuring properly is exactly what lets you make decisions.

u30l4-10.prompt: What should you take into account to measure your return honestly? Select all that apply.
options: Compare it with a benchmark index
Look only at your best year
u30l4-10.explanation: Your best year says little: what matters is the net result, over the long term and against an alternative.

u30l5-1.prompt: Put the first sections of an Investment Policy Statement in order.
u30l5-1.explanation: First what and by when; then with what emergency fund, how to allocate and with which products.

u30l5-2.prompt: You review the Statement once a year or when your ____ changes, not when the market changes.
u30l5-2.explanation: A new job or a child changes your goals; a stock market fall doesn't.

u30l5-3.prompt: Which point in the Statement protects you most from panic?
options: What you'll do if the market falls 30 %
u30l5-3.explanation: You decide it calmly and remind yourself of it when everyone is selling.

u30l5-4.prompt: What can go in the «what I'll never do» section? Select all that apply.
options: Put more than 20 % into a single asset
u30l5-4.explanation: Contributing every month is part of the plan, not something to avoid.

u30l5-5.prompt: Does it go in your Statement or not?
options: I contribute €200 on the 1st of every month
Where the IBEX will be in December
u30l5-5.explanation: The plan sets out rules you control, not predictions or trends.
right: Yes, it goes in the plan

u30l5-6.prompt: Your Statement says that at most 5 % of your wealth will go on speculation. You have €18,000. What's the maximum?
u30l5-6.explanation: 18,000 × 0.05 = €900, and only money you could afford to lose entirely.

u30l5-7.prompt: If the stock market rises a lot two years in a row, you should rewrite your Statement with more shares.
u30l5-7.explanation: Changing the plan because of what the market did is exactly what the Statement is trying to prevent.

u30l5-8.prompt: Bruno's Statement says 80 % shares and 20 % bonds. After two very good years, he wants to go 100 % shares «because bonds don't earn anything». What do you tell him?
options: That he should move everything into bonds just in case
That he should do it: the market is rising
That he should reread why he chose 80/20 and, if his life hasn't changed, stick with it
u30l5-8.explanation: The Statement changes with your life, not with the market.
feedback: Changing out of fear isn't following the plan either.
Raising your risk after the rises is buying euphoria. His plan already took into account that bonds earn less.
Good: the plan exists so you don't decide with the emotion of the moment.

u30l5-9.prompt: Writing your plan while calm helps you avoid deciding in the middle of a panic.
u30l5-9.explanation: That's its main purpose: separating the decision from the moment of fear.

u30l5-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: I don't sell, I keep contributing, I rebalance if needed and I reread the plan
I take out a loan to buy more
Sell everything and come back when things calm down
u30l5-10.explanation: Point 8 of the plan exists for this very moment.
feedback: That's what having a plan looks like! And in falls like this, rebalancing makes you buy cheap.
Your Statement probably says «never with borrowed money». For good reason.
You didn't decide that calmly: fear is deciding for you.
lines: The stock market has dropped 30 % 😱 Everyone's selling.
What does your Investment Policy Statement say?

u30l6-1.prompt: Allocate the €10,000. Rules: at least 4 products, none above 60 %, at least 15 % in bonds, at most 10 % in gold, 10 % in a single share and 5 % in crypto.
options: Global bond fund hedged to euros
u30l6-1.explanation: A diversified, cheap core, a cushion of bonds for the falls and the speculative part kept limited. You can lose everything in crypto. Educational example, not a recommendation.

u30l6-2.prompt: You've set aside a small slice for speculation. You want to trade the IBEX 35 without risking more than 1 % of your €10,000 (€100). Choose the amount and place the stop.
u30l6-2.explanation: The speculative part has rules too: the stop and the size decide how much you can lose, not the market.

u30l6-3.prompt: Year one: the stock market falls 25 % and your portfolio 18 %. A friend tells you to sell everything. What do you do?
options: Move everything into bitcoin to recover quickly
Follow the plan: contribute, rebalance into shares if needed and don't sell
u30l6-3.explanation: Bonds cushioned the fall (−18 % versus −25 %). Now it's time for point 8 of your plan.
feedback: Chasing the recovery with more risk usually makes the hole deeper.
Good: with a 20-year horizon, a bad year is part of the journey.
Turning a fall into a permanent loss is the most expensive mistake in market history.

u30l6-4.prompt: A colleague tells you: «Sell the bonds and put everything into the share that's risen most this year». What do you reply?
options: That my portfolio has an allocation chosen for 20 years and I don't chase trends
That I'll think about it if it rises another 20 %
I take their advice: bonds don't earn anything
u30l6-4.explanation: Diversifying means giving up on picking the star of the year in exchange for not depending on it.
feedback: That's how you defend a portfolio: with the plan, not with the latest headline.
Waiting for it to rise further before getting in is the same mistake, just later.
Bonds are there for the falls, not to earn more. And chasing whatever rose most usually arrives late.

u30l6-5.prompt: Which argument best defends a diversified portfolio?
options: «It holds thousands of companies, has low costs and an allocation I can stick with in a fall»
«An influencer says it's going to go up»
«Last year it rose more than my cousin's»
u30l6-5.explanation: Diversification, cost and tolerance for falls: the things you can control.

u30l6-6.prompt: Your portfolio: 60 % in a fund at 0.20 %, 20 % in emerging markets at 0.30 % and 20 % in bonds at 0.15 %. How many euros a year do you pay on €10,000?

u30l6-7.prompt: What should your €10,000 portfolio over 20 years have? Select all that apply.
options: A big bet on the latest trend
u30l6-7.explanation: The speculative part, if there is one, small and limited.

u30l6-8.prompt: A €10,000 portfolio needs at least 15 products to be diversified.
u30l6-8.explanation: With one to three index funds you already own thousands of companies from all over the world.

u30l6-9.prompt: Put the steps for getting your portfolio up and running in order.
options: Have your emergency fund set aside
u30l6-9.explanation: First the foundation and the key decision; then the products and the discipline.

u30l6-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Because the stock market always goes up
Because I've picked whatever will rise most
I don't know if it'll go up this year, but it's diversified, it's cheap and I know what I'll do in a fall
u30l6-10.explanation: You defend a portfolio with diversification, costs and a plan, not with predictions.
feedback: Over the long term it has gone up, but with falls of up to 50 % along the way.
Nobody knows what will rise most. A portfolio that depends on guessing right is fragile.
Perfect defence! You talked about what you control, not what you're guessing.
lines: Go on then, defend your portfolio 🧐
Why do you think it's going to work?
